questions.question_text: Use $(1+x)^{5}(1+x)^{5}=(1+x)^{10}$ to prove that $\sum_{r=0}^{5}({^{5}C_{r}})^{2}={^{10}C_{5}}$. Which option gives a valid proof?

options.text: Expanding both factors, the coefficient of $x^{5}$ on LHS is $\sum_{r=0}^{5}{^{5}C_{r}}{^{5}C_{5-r}}=\sum_{r=0}^{5}({^{5}C_{r}})^{2}$ by symmetry. On RHS it is $^{10}C_{5}$, so equating coefficients proves the identity.
Set $x=1$. Both sides equal $1024$, so the sum of squared coefficients equals $^{10}C_{5}$.
options.why: Substitution sums all coefficients of the product; it does not isolate the products contributing to $x^{5}$.

options.text: The coefficient of $x^{5}$ on LHS is ${^{5}C_{0}}{^{5}C_{5}}$. On RHS it is $^{10}C_{5}$, so the identity follows.
options.why: Includes only one pair of terms and omits the other five pairs whose powers add to $5$.

options.text: The coefficient of $x^{5}$ on LHS is $\sum_{r=0}^{5}({^{5}C_{r}})^{2}$. On RHS it is $^{5}C_{5}$, so equating coefficients proves the identity.
options.why: Uses the coefficient from exponent $5$ instead of the RHS exponent $10$.

questions.solution_text:
Expand the two factors in $(1+x)^{5}(1+x)^{5}=(1+x)^{10}$.
The coefficient of $x^{5}$ on LHS is $\sum_{r=0}^{5}{^{5}C_{r}}{^{5}C_{5-r}}=\sum_{r=0}^{5}({^{5}C_{r}})^{2}$ by symmetry.
On RHS the coefficient is $^{10}C_{5}$. Equating coefficients proves the supplied identity.

options.text: Expanding the factors gives coefficient of $x^{3}$ equal to ${^{2}C_{0}}{^{7}C_{3}}+{^{2}C_{1}}{^{7}C_{2}}+{^{2}C_{2}}{^{7}C_{1}}$. The boundary coefficients in row $2$ equal $1$; equating this with the RHS coefficient $^{9}C_{3}$ proves the identity.

options.why: Keeps the second index fixed at $3$, so the last two products have powers $4$ and $5$.

options.text: The coefficient of $x^{3}$ on LHS is ${^{7}C_{3}}+{^{2}C_{1}}{^{7}C_{2}}$. Equate it with $^{9}C_{3}$.
options.why: Omits the product of the $x^{2}$ term in the first factor and the $x$ term in the second.

options.text: Set $x=1$ to obtain $512=512$. This proves the supplied product-sum identity.
options.why: The substitution compares the sums of all coefficients, rather than the required coefficient of $x^{3}$.

questions.solution_text:
Expand both factors and collect terms whose powers add to $3$.
The LHS coefficient is ${^{2}C_{0}}{^{7}C_{3}}+{^{2}C_{1}}{^{7}C_{2}}+{^{2}C_{2}}{^{7}C_{1}}={^{7}C_{3}}+{^{2}C_{1}}{^{7}C_{2}}+{^{7}C_{1}}$.
The RHS coefficient is $^{9}C_{3}$. Equating coefficients proves the identity.

questions.question_text: Use $(1+x)^{3}(1+x)^{6}=(1+x)^{9}$ to prove that $\sum_{r=0}^{3}{^{3}C_{r}}{^{6}C_{4-r}}={^{9}C_{4}}$. Which option gives a valid proof?

options.text: Expand the two factors. Products contribute to $x^{4}$ when their indices add to $4$, giving $\sum_{r=0}^{3}{^{3}C_{r}}{^{6}C_{4-r}}$. The RHS coefficient is $^{9}C_{4}$, so equating coefficients proves the identity.
The coefficient of $x^{9}$ on both sides is $1$, so the supplied identity follows.
options.why: Compares the leading coefficients, which do not give the supplied sum.

options.text: Set $x=1$ to obtain $512=512$, which proves the supplied identity.
options.why: Compares the sums of all coefficients and does not isolate the coefficient of $x^{4}$.

options.text: Replace the product by $(1+x)^{3}(1-x)^{6}=(1-x^{2})^{9}$ and equate coefficients of $x^{4}$.
options.why: Uses a false product identity and introduces alternating signs. In general, $(1+x)^{m}(1-x)^{n}=(1-x^{2})^{m+n}$ also fails when $m=n>0$, since the product then equals $(1-x^{2})^{m}$.

questions.solution_text:
In the expanded product, $x^{r}x^{s}=x^{4}$ when $r+s=4$.
The first factor has $0\leq r\leq3$, giving $1\leq s=4-r\leq4$, all valid indices in row $6$.
The LHS coefficient is $\sum_{r=0}^{3}{^{3}C_{r}}{^{6}C_{4-r}}$ and the RHS coefficient is $^{9}C_{4}$. Equating them proves the identity.

questions.question_text: Use $(1+x)^{6}(1+x)^{6}=(1+x)^{12}$ to prove that $\sum_{r=0}^{6}({^{6}C_{r}})^{2}={^{12}C_{6}}$. Which option gives a valid proof?

options.text: The expanded LHS has coefficient of $x^{6}$ equal to $\sum_{r=0}^{6}{^{6}C_{r}}{^{6}C_{6-r}}=\sum_{r=0}^{6}({^{6}C_{r}})^{2}$ by symmetry. The RHS coefficient is $^{12}C_{6}$; equating them proves the identity.
Square each term of $(1+x)^{6}$ separately. The coefficient of $x^{6}$ is then $({^{6}C_{3}})^{2}$, which proves the identity.
options.why: Omits cross-products when squaring the expansion.

options.text: Add the coefficients of $(1+x)^{6}$ to obtain $64$. This equals the sum of their squares and proves the identity.
options.why: Confuses the sum of coefficients with the sum of their squares.

options.text: The LHS coefficient of $x^{6}$ is the sum of squares. Equate it with the RHS coefficient of $x^{5}$, namely $^{12}C_{5}$.
options.why: Compares coefficients of different powers.

questions.solution_text:
Expand both factors. The coefficient of $x^{6}$ on LHS is $\sum_{r=0}^{6}{^{6}C_{r}}{^{6}C_{6-r}}$.
Symmetry changes this to $\sum_{r=0}^{6}({^{6}C_{r}})^{2}$.
The coefficient of $x^{6}$ on RHS is $^{12}C_{6}$. Equating coefficients proves the identity.

options.text: Expanding both factors gives coefficient of $x^{2}$ equal to ${^{3}C_{0}}{^{5}C_{2}}+{^{3}C_{1}}{^{5}C_{1}}+{^{3}C_{2}}{^{5}C_{0}}$. Using the boundary coefficients $1$ and equating this with $^{8}C_{2}$ proves the identity.
The LHS coefficient of $x^{2}$ is ${^{5}C_{2}}+{^{3}C_{2}}$. Equate it with $^{8}C_{2}$.
options.why: Omits the product of the two $x$ terms.
Adds the two coefficients of $x$ instead of multiplying them.

options.text: The LHS coefficient is the supplied sum. Since the exponents multiply to $15$, equate it with $^{15}C_{2}$.
options.why: Multiplies the exponents instead of adding them when combining powers with the same base.

questions.solution_text:
The coefficient of $x^{2}$ in the expanded product is ${^{3}C_{0}}{^{5}C_{2}}+{^{3}C_{1}}{^{5}C_{1}}+{^{3}C_{2}}{^{5}C_{0}}$.
Since $^{3}C_{0}={^{5}C_{0}}=1$, this equals the supplied LHS.
The coefficient of $x^{2}$ in $(1+x)^{8}$ is $^{8}C_{2}$. Equating coefficients proves the identity.

options.text: Expand both factors. The coefficient of $x^{2}$ on LHS is ${^{4}C_{2}}{^{6}C_{0}}+{^{4}C_{1}}{^{6}C_{1}}+{^{4}C_{0}}{^{6}C_{2}}$, which simplifies to the supplied sum. Equate it with the RHS coefficient $^{10}C_{2}$.
The supplied sum is the LHS coefficient of $x^{2}$. Equate it with $^{10}C_{3}$ on RHS.
options.why: Uses the coefficient of $x^{3}$ on RHS instead of $x^{2}$.

options.text: Expand the product as $(1+x)^{24}$. Its coefficient of $x^{2}$ is $^{24}C_{2}$, proving the identity.
options.why: Multiplies the exponents $4$ and $6$ instead of adding them.

options.text: The LHS coefficient of $x^{2}$ is ${^{4}C_{2}}+{^{4}C_{1}}{^{6}C_{1}}$. Equate it with $^{10}C_{2}$.
options.why: Omits the constant term of the first factor multiplied by the $x^{2}$ term of the second.

questions.question_text: For a positive integer $m$, use $\left(x+\frac{1}{x}\right)^{2m}\left(x+\frac{1}{x}\right)^{2m}=\left(x+\frac{1}{x}\right)^{4m}$ to prove that $\sum_{r=0}^{2m}({^{2m}C_{r}})^{2}={^{4m}C_{2m}}$. Which option gives a valid proof?

options.text: For $x\ne0$, the RHS general term is ${^{4m}C_{t}}x^{4m-2t}$, giving constant term $^{4m}C_{2m}$. LHS exponents sum to zero when $r+s=2m$, giving $\sum_{r=0}^{2m}{^{2m}C_{r}}{^{2m}C_{2m-r}}=\sum_{r=0}^{2m}({^{2m}C_{r}})^{2}$ by symmetry. Equating constant terms proves the identity.
The RHS constant term is $^{4m}C_{2m}$. On LHS, equal exponents give a constant, so every pair with $r=s$ contributes its squared coefficient and proves the identity.
options.why: Equal exponents do not generally sum to zero; constant products require $r+s=2m$, not merely $r=s$.

options.text: The RHS constant term is $^{4m}C_{m}$. The LHS constant term is the supplied sum by symmetry, so equating them proves the identity.
options.why: Solves $4m-2t=0$ incorrectly as $t=m$ instead of $t=2m$.

options.text: Set $x=1$ to obtain $2^{4m}=2^{4m}$. This proves that the supplied sum equals the constant term.
options.why: Substitution sums all terms and does not isolate constant terms.

questions.solution_text:
Take $x\ne0$. On RHS, ${^{4m}C_{t}}x^{4m-2t}$ is constant when $t=2m$, giving $^{4m}C_{2m}$.
On LHS, terms indexed by $r,s$ have combined exponent $4m-2r-2s$, which is zero when $r+s=2m$.
The constant term is $\sum_{r=0}^{2m}{^{2m}C_{r}}{^{2m}C_{2m-r}}=\sum_{r=0}^{2m}({^{2m}C_{r}})^{2}$ by symmetry.
Equating constant terms proves the identity.
